title: Trees, Waves and Subgroups
description: Where language family trees came from, what counts as evidence for a branch, and when history is not a tree

concepts.title: Schleicher's Tree and Darwin's Parallels
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1853 the German linguist August Schleicher published two articles containing his first family trees of languages: one for Germanic and Balto-Slavic, and one for the whole Indo-European family. He may have borrowed the picture from a colleague, the Czech linguist František Ladislav Čelakovský, whose lectures, published after his death, contain an early tree diagram of the Slavic languages.1 Schleicher was very interested in biology, especially botany, and he liked to compare languages with organisms that pass through birth, youth, old age and death.2

Six years later the only figure in Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) was also a tree, and in The Descent of Man (1871) Darwin pointed to "curious parallels" between biological and linguistic evolution. The parallels run deep, which is why biologists and linguists keep meeting the same problems:

  • Words pass from parents to children much as genes do, and both change a little in every generation.
  • Cognates, words descended from one ancestral word, play the role of homologous genes.
  • Borrowing between languages resembles lateral gene transfer between microbes.
  • Language death resembles extinction, and dialects drifting apart resemble populations splitting into species.

A tree is more than a picture. It is a hypothesis with testable content: it says which languages share a more recent common ancestor than any of them shares with outsiders, and in what order the splits happened. That content is exactly what the rest of this topic tries to estimate, date and map. It is also what critics attack, because a tree assumes that once two speech communities part, they stop exchanging material. As early as 1948 the American anthropologist Kroeber explicitly contrasted Darwin's idea of a tree of life with that of a tree of cultures,3 and the question of how tree-like human history really is has never gone away.

concepts.title: Shared Innovations Make a Branch
concepts.contentHtml:
The comparative method you met in Historical Linguistics shows that languages are related and reconstructs their ancestor. A second question is harder: inside a family, which languages form a branch together? The classical answer is shared innovations: changes that happened once, in a common ancestor, and were inherited by all of its descendants. Subgrouping by shared innovations dates back to the end of the nineteenth century.1 The consonant shift described by Grimm's law is the textbook case. Every Germanic language shows it and no other branch does, so it points to a single Proto-Germanic ancestor.

The first trap is the shared retention. Latin, Greek and Sanskrit all keep features that Proto-Indo-European already had, but keeping an old feature says nothing about a closer relationship, because every branch started with it. Biologists draw the same line between shared derived characters and shared ancestral ones. The second trap is parallel innovation: natural changes can happen independently in several languages. When Laurent Sagart and colleagues built dated trees for Sino-Tibetan in 2019, they concluded that similarities in verb morphology once offered as evidence for certain subgroups more likely reflect a mix of retentions and parallel innovations.2

Convincing subgroups rest on specific, unusual changes. In Austronesian, the Central Pacific subgroup is defined partly by the loss of the Proto-Oceanic uvular trill *R, and Central-Eastern Malayo-Polynesian partly by the lowering of high vowels in certain morphemes.3 Classifications like these give quantitative methods something independent to be checked against. Simon Greenhill, Alexei Drummond and Russell Gray reported that their Bayesian trees of 400 Austronesian languages, built from basic vocabulary, supported 26 of the 34 main subgroups proposed by historical linguists.4 They later measured the distance between their sampled trees and the standard classification: a median of 0.223 on a normalised scale, against 0.685 for random trees. When methods that use different evidence (sound changes for the linguists, basic vocabulary for the trees) agree, that is one of the strongest arguments that both are tracking real history.

concepts.title: Waves, Dialect Chains and Networks
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1872 Johannes Schmidt pointed out that linguistic data contradicted the idea of simple, tree-like splitting. His wave theory (Wellentheorie) states that certain changes spread like waves in concentric circles over neighbouring speech communities, so that neighbouring branches share innovations cutting across any tree. Before Schmidt, Hugo Schuchardt had already stressed that languages diverge gradually while still influencing each other.1 Textbooks now usually present the tree and the wave as two complementary models, each showing one side of language history.2

The commonest source of wave-like signal is a dialect chain. A language spreads across a region, its dialects stay in contact, and innovations spread over overlapping areas. When the chain later breaks into separate languages, they inherit crossing, conflicting patterns that no single tree can fit. Working from linguistic evidence, Pawley argued in 1996 that the settlement of Polynesia involved the establishment and break-up of a whole series of dialect chains.3

Rather than assume a tree, you can measure how tree-like the data are. NeighborNet draws split graphs that display conflicting signal instead of hiding it, and delta scores average how far each set of four languages departs from a perfect tree; higher means less tree-like. Gray, David Bryant and Greenhill tried this on 12 Indo-European languages including Sranan, a creole of Surinam with words from both English and Dutch. The set scored 0.23 overall, and Sranan, with its mixed history, scored highest at 0.29.4 Then came a surprise. The far-flung Polynesian islands were settled only in the last 3,000 years, so you might expect a clean tree, yet Polynesian basic vocabulary averaged 0.41 against 0.22 for Indo-European. The voyaging skills of the Polynesians meant that ocean distances were no barrier to ongoing contact.5 How tree-like a family is turns out to be an empirical question, and it matters, because every dating method in the lessons ahead assumes a tree.

title: Lexicostatistics and the Fall of Glottochronology
description: Swadesh's word lists, a decay clock for vocabulary, and why the clock broke

concepts.title: Counting Cognates: Swadesh's Lists
concepts.contentHtml:
In the early 1950s the linguist Morris Swadesh proposed comparing languages on a fixed list of basic meanings: 200 concepts in 1952, trimmed to 100 in 1955.1 The idea was that words for things every community talks about (body parts, low numbers, everyday actions such as eating and dying) are stable and resistant to borrowing, so when two languages share a related word for one of them, inheritance is the likely reason. The resistance is only relative: about 10% of the Swadesh 100-word list is still prone to borrowing.2

Lexicostatistics turns the list into numbers. You collect the word for each meaning in each language, decide which pairs are cognate using the sound correspondences of the comparative method, and count the percentage of the list that is cognate for every pair of languages. High percentages mean close relatives, and the matrix of percentages can be clustered into a tree. Swadesh lists have been used to build many large datasets of Indo-European and Austronesian languages, and later scholars proposed even shorter lists, of 40, 35, 33 or only 15 concepts, chosen largely by linguistic intuition and experience.3

Notice what a single percentage throws away. Two pairs of languages can each share 60% of the list but share a different 60%, and the pattern of which words are shared is exactly what tells you about branches and shared innovations. A percentage also hides judgement calls. Deciding that two words are cognate takes expert work, experts can disagree, and an undetected loanword quietly inflates the score. Keep these weaknesses in mind: the methods in Lesson 3 keep Swadesh's lists but use the full pattern of cognates rather than one number per pair of languages.

concepts.title: Glottochronology: A Decay Clock for Words
concepts.contentHtml:
Swadesh hoped to date language splits the way a physicist dates a sample by its decay. Suppose basic vocabulary is replaced at a constant average rate, so that a fraction r of the list survives each millennium. A single language keeps \(r^t\) of its list after t millennia. Two languages that split from one ancestor each lose words independently, so the fraction they still share, C, falls twice as fast. Solving for time gives the formula of glottochronology, which Swadesh set out in 1950: the time depth equals the logarithm of C divided by twice the logarithm of r.

The constant generally used for the 100-word list was a retention rate of 86% per millennium.1 Run the numbers. Two languages that split 1,000 years ago should share about 0.86 × 0.86, or 74%, of their list.2 Two languages sharing only half their list would have split about 2,300 years ago, because 0.86 raised to the power 4.6 is about 0.5, and 4.6 millennia of loss shared between two lineages is 2.3 millennia each.

The appeal was enormous. The method needed only a short word list, no written records and a little arithmetic, and it promised dates for families with no history at all. But the arithmetic rests on three hidden assumptions:

  • every language replaces its basic vocabulary at the same rate;
  • every meaning on the list is replaced at the same rate;
  • cognates are identified correctly and loanwords removed.

Swadesh himself wrote of a constant average rate, and the linguist Jacques Guy later pointed out the oddity: it would be quite unreasonable for every language family to split only when its average rate happened to equal one constant value.3 The only coherent reading is that rates fluctuate within narrow limits. The next concept shows what happened when people checked.

concepts.title: Why the Clock Broke
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1962 Bergsland and Vogt tested glottochronology on closely related languages and dialects and found that retention rates varied enormously.1 One pair was East and West Greenlandic, two closely related varieties, which kept 53.7% and 97.2% of the list per millennium respectively.2 Guy spelled out the consequence. Two languages that split 1,000 years ago should share about 74% of their list at the standard rate, but at the Greenlandic rates they would share about 52%. On a 100-word list those two figures are about four standard deviations apart, so no reasonable error bar can rescue the method.

The second assumption failed too. In 1965 Dyen, James and Cole calculated retention rates for the individual items on a standard list and found that those varied as well.3 Much later, Mark Pagel and colleagues showed how wide the spread is: across Indo-European, 'two' is expressed by one related word everywhere, while 'tail' is expressed by dozens of unrelated words. Mixing fast and slow words breaks the formula in a subtle way. Take Guy's example, with half the list keeping 90% per period and half keeping 10%. After one period 50% survives, so a single-rate clock predicts 25% after two periods and 12.5% after three. The real figures are 41% and 36.5%, because the slow words come to dominate what is left.4 A clock tuned on young splits therefore makes old splits look far too young.

Guy judged that Bergsland and Vogt's study should have brought about drastic, if painful, revisions in the lexicostatistical method, and that it was ignored.5 Glottochronology lost credibility as these problems mounted, but its ingredients did not vanish. Cognate-coded basic vocabulary is still the raw material of computational work, and the idea that change accumulates with time still underlies every date. What changed was the model: modern methods let rates vary between words and between lineages, calibrate against known dates, and report their uncertainty openly.

title: Phylogenetics Borrowed from Biology
description: Coding cognates as characters, models of word gain and loss, and dating trees with relaxed clocks

concepts.title: Words as Characters
concepts.contentHtml:
Bayesian phylolinguistics keeps Swadesh's lists but throws away the percentages. Take the meaning 'tail': Greek ourá, German Schwanz, French queue and English tail are unrelated words. Each group of related words for a meaning forms a cognate set, and each cognate set becomes a column in a data matrix. A language scores 1 in a column if its word for that meaning belongs to the set and 0 if not. This binary presence or absence coding turns vocabulary lists into something a phylogenetic program can read, much as it reads the bases of DNA. Russell Gray and Quentin Atkinson's 2003 analysis of Indo-European used a matrix of 87 languages with 2,449 lexical items coded this way.1

The model treats language change as the gain and loss of cognates along the branches of a tree. A new word for 'tail' appears once, in one lineage, and is inherited by that lineage's descendants; it can later be lost again in different branches. The stochastic Dollo model of Nicholls and Gray builds in this asymmetry directly: a cognate can evolve only once but be lost multiple times.2 Other teams use a covarion model, which Rebecca Grollemund and colleagues found well suited to binary coded cognate data, again because each cognate class ideally arises just once on the tree.

Everything depends on the cognate judgements, and people make them. Expert opinion on cognate classes can differ, much as biologists can disagree about how to align gene sequences, so careful studies rerun their analyses on alternative codings to check that the results hold.3 Borrowings must be identified and removed, or they will masquerade as inheritance. Coding problems were serious enough in Indo-European that in 2023 a team led by Paul Heggarty built a new database designed to eliminate past inconsistencies in cognate coding.4 Good phylogenetics starts with good comparative linguistics.

concepts.title: Likelihood, Priors and the Posterior
concepts.contentHtml:
Given a matrix, which tree produced it? Bayesian inference answers with Bayes' theorem: the probability of a tree given the data is proportional to the probability of the data given the tree (the likelihood) multiplied by the prior probability of the tree. The likelihood comes from a model of how 0s and 1s flip along branches over time, a continuous-time Markov process of the kind used for DNA. The prior encodes assumptions about tree shapes, branch lengths and rates. Models are compared by how well they fit: in a 2015 study of Bantu, a plain two-state model was clearly beaten by a covarion model.

You cannot simply check every tree. For just 20 languages there are about \(8 \times 10^{21}\) possible rooted trees. Instead, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) takes a random walk through tree space, proposing small changes and accepting them in a way that makes the time spent near each tree proportional to its posterior probability. The output is not one tree but a posterior sample. MCMC sampling is run to obtain a sample of plausible trees from the posterior distribution,1 4,200 of them in Gray, Drummond and Greenhill's Austronesian analysis. A branch's support is simply the share of sampled trees that contain it, and dates come as 95% highest posterior density intervals, such as 4,750–5,800 years for the Austronesian root.2

To compare hypotheses, phylolinguists use Bayes factors, which compare the posterior odds of one hypothesis against another with their prior odds. On the scale used by Remco Bouckaert's team, a Bayes factor of 5–20 is taken as substantial support, over 20 as strong support, and over 100 as decisive.3 The great virtue of the approach is that uncertainty becomes part of the answer. If the data cannot decide between two branchings, the posterior sample contains both, and every later conclusion, from dates to homelands, can be averaged over that uncertainty instead of resting on one guessed tree.

concepts.title: Clocks and Calibrations
concepts.contentHtml:
A tree built from cognate data measures branch lengths in expected changes, not years. To convert, you need calibrations: languages or ancestral nodes whose ages are known from outside evidence, entered as priors on the tree. For their 2019 study of Sino-Tibetan, Sagart and colleagues used the dates of the earliest texts: Old Chinese at 2,800–2,300 years before present, Old Tibetan at 1,200, Tangut at 900 and Old Burmese at 800.1 Austronesian studies use dates for reconstructed ancestors, placing Proto-Oceanic around 3,300 years ago and Proto-Austronesian around 5,200, each with a stated uncertainty.2

The clock itself can be strict or relaxed. A strict clock is glottochronology's assumption that every lineage changes at the same rate. A relaxed clock assumes that rates can vary freely across the tree, so a conservative branch and a fast-changing one can sit side by side; separate settings let rates vary between meanings too. When Greenhill and colleagues compared clock models for 81 Austronesian languages in 2017, relaxed clocks fitted far better than strict ones.3 So the modern method keeps the intuition that change piles up with time while dropping the fixed rate that sank glottochronology.

Calibrations are also the method's soft spot. An archaeological date for a proto-language is an inference, not a record. Heggarty objected that one deep-time study rested on just two calibration points, neither historically known, only hypothetical matches with archaeology.4 Good studies therefore test sensitivity. When Greenhill, Drummond and Gray re-dated Austronesian with only the most robust calibrations, the mean root age came out at 5,117 years, with an interval of 4,660–5,680, close to their earlier estimate. The Sino-Tibetan trees, for their part, placed that family's origin with north Chinese millet farmers around 7,200 years ago.5 As the next lesson shows, the Indo-European fight is largely about whether the calibrations, the coding and the model can be trusted.

title: Indo-European on a Bayesian Clock
description: Gray and Atkinson's 2003 dates, the 2012 map of the homeland, and the ancestry-constraint backlash

concepts.title: Gray and Atkinson 2003: An Anatolian Date
concepts.contentHtml:
The origin of Indo-European has been called "the most intensively studied, yet still most recalcitrant, problem of historical linguistics".1 Two hypotheses led the field. The Kurgan or steppe hypothesis, associated with Gimbutas, links the family to an expansion into Europe and the Near East by Kurgan horsemen beginning in the sixth millennium before present. The Anatolian hypothesis, associated with Colin Renfrew, holds that Indo-European languages expanded with the spread of agriculture from Anatolia around 8,000–9,500 years ago. Each ties the languages to a known archaeological expansion, and each had serious defenders.

The two ideas make different predictions about time: roughly 6,000 years for the steppe against 8,000–9,500 for Anatolia. So a date alone can test them, with no map needed. In 2003 Russell Gray and Quentin Atkinson analysed a matrix of 87 languages with 2,449 lexical items using Bayesian methods borrowed from evolutionary biology. Their analysis produced an estimated age range for the initial Indo-European divergence of between 7,800 and 9,800 years ago, in what they called striking agreement with the Anatolian hypothesis.2 The results were robust to changes in coding procedures, calibration points, the rooting of the trees and the priors.3

Why did the paper land so hard? Glottochronology's failure had left many linguists distrustful of any date drawn from vocabulary. Gray and Atkinson's method answered the old objections directly: rates could vary across words and branches, uncertainty was explicit, and the tree was estimated rather than assumed. Published in Nature, it set off a debate that still runs. Critics questioned the cognate coding, the way ancient languages were placed in the tree, and the conversion of vocabulary change into years. Those objections, and the attempts to answer them, fill the next two concepts and the whole of Lesson 5.

concepts.title: Mapping the Homeland: Bouckaert and Colleagues, 2012
concepts.contentHtml:
A date alone cannot put a homeland on a map, so in 2012 Remco Bouckaert, Quentin Atkinson and colleagues borrowed a tool from epidemiology. Bayesian phylogeography had been developed to investigate the origin of virus outbreaks from molecular sequence data. The team adapted it to basic vocabulary and geographic ranges for 103 ancient and contemporary Indo-European languages.1 Each language's location is treated as a continuous vector (longitude and latitude) that evolves along the branches by a relaxed random walk, so the model infers the tree and the most probable locations of its ancestors at the same time.

The root landed in Anatolia, in present-day Turkey. Bayes factors comparing an Anatolian root with two versions of the steppe homeland were 175 and 159.3, well into the decisive range, and the root's age came out at 7,116–10,410 years ago.2 The team ran several checks:

  • The geographic centre of the sampled languages lies within the steppe region, so the model was not simply returning the centre of mass.
  • The model placed the most recent common ancestor of the Romance languages around Rome, as history says it should.3
  • Making movement into water 100 times less likely than movement over land still favoured Anatolia.
  • Analyses of only the ancient languages, or only the contemporary ones (which leaves out the extinct Anatolian branch), still favoured Anatolia.

The authors did not claim that farming explained everything. In their tree, the five major subfamilies, Celtic, Germanic, Italic, Balto-Slavic and Indo-Iranian, all emerged as distinct lineages between 4,000 and 6,000 years ago, at the same time as later cultural expansions including the Kurgan one.4 Even the strongest Anatolian result left room for movements off the steppe.

concepts.title: The Backlash: Ancestry Constraints
concepts.contentHtml:
The sharpest reply came from Berkeley. In 2015 Will Chang, Chundra Cathcart, David Hall and Andrew Garrett pointed out that for some languages we can watch the descent happen. Latin did not merely sit beside the Romance languages as a sister; it was their ancestor. Earlier analyses treated ancient and medieval languages as tips of the tree, like their descendants. Chang's team added ancestry constraints, placing such languages directly ancestral to their modern descendants, so that the model could learn rates of change from changes actually observed between, say, Latin and Spanish.

With those constraints, the result strongly supported the steppe hypothesis.1 The analysis also found that homoplasy, the same trait arising independently more than once, is common in lexical traits, contrary to the assumptions of earlier work. Lexical traits recur because of recurring patterns of semantic and morphological change.2 The logic of the date shift is simple. If observed ancestor and descendant pairs show change happening faster than the model had assumed, the same amount of difference needs less time to build up, and the root moves younger.

Other critics pointed to checks that failed. Heggarty noted that the 2012 trees put the split between Portuguese and Spanish far too late, centred on AD 1500.3 Then, in 2023, Heggarty and more than thirty co-authors answered with a rebuilt database that removed past inconsistencies in cognate coding, analysed with trees that allow ancient languages to be ancestors without forcing them to be. That analysis indicated that few ancient languages are direct ancestors of modern clades, which undercuts the case for forcing them into that role, and it put the root at about 8,120 years ago.4 Both sides use the same family of methods. The disagreement lies in coding, sampling and assumptions, which is exactly where you should look whenever two models give different dates.

title: Steppe, Genes and the Hybrid Hypothesis
description: Reading culture from reconstructed words, what ancient DNA added, and the search for Proto-Indo-Anatolian

concepts.title: Linguistic Palaeontology
concepts.contentHtml:
Linguistic palaeontology uses words reconstructed for a proto-language to make inferences about its speakers' culture and environment. The logic is appealing: if a word for something can be traced back to Proto-Indo-European, its speakers presumably knew that thing. It is central to the steppe case. To its supporters, qualitative evidence from reconstructed vocabulary, together with correlations with archaeology, suggests that Indo-European began on the Pontic-Caspian steppe and spread with cultural innovations associated with pastoralism, beginning about 6,500–5,500 years ago.1

The best-known version concerns transport. The steppe hypothesis proposes that early Indo-European speakers were pastoralists of the grasslands north of the Black and Caspian Seas, and that their languages spread into Europe after the invention of wheeled vehicles.2 Supporters argue that inherited vocabulary for wheeled vehicles means the proto-language cannot be older than the wheel, which, if true, sets a ceiling on its age. A second line of argument points to possible early borrowings between Indo-European and the Uralic family of northern Eurasia.3

Critics reply that the reliability of these inferences remains controversial,4 and you can see why:

  • A word's meaning can shift. A reconstructed root may once have meant something more general and acquired its technical sense only later.
  • Words that spread by borrowing between languages that had already separated, the wave-like process from Lesson 1, can masquerade as inheritance.
  • The first branch matters. The Anatolian languages, such as Hittite, are traditionally treated as the first split, so vocabulary missing from Anatolian may date only the later core of the family, not its root.

That last point has become central, and a newer terminology reflects it: some researchers now call the whole group Indo-Anatolian and reserve Indo-European for the non-Anatolian branches. Linguistic palaeontology and Bayesian dating pointed in different directions, and neither could settle the matter alone. A third line of evidence was needed.

concepts.title: What Ancient DNA Added
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2015 a team led by Wolfgang Haak, Iosif Lazaridis and David Reich published genome-wide data from 69 Europeans who lived between 8,000 and 3,000 years ago, enriching their ancient DNA for a target set of almost 400,000 genetic positions.1 Two movements stood out. Around 8,000–7,000 years ago, closely related groups of early farmers, different from the local hunter-gatherers, appeared in Germany, Hungary and Spain. Then, about 4,500 years ago, the Late Neolithic Corded Ware people of Germany traced about 75% of their ancestry to the Yamnaya steppe herders, whose own ancestry combined eastern European hunter-gatherers with a population of Near Eastern ancestry.2

The authors called this a massive migration into the heartland of Europe from its eastern periphery. The Corded Ware were genetically closest to Yamnaya people about 2,600 km away, and steppe ancestry is ubiquitous in present-day Europeans. The results, they wrote, provide support for a steppe origin of at least some of the Indo-European languages of Europe. Notice that both movements happened. Early farmers and, later, steppe herders each reshaped Europe's population, so DNA alone does not choose between the hypotheses; it sharpens the question of which migration carried which languages.

Keep the limits in view. The authors themselves noted that ancient DNA is silent on the languages spoken by preliterate populations; it carries evidence only about the migrations that theories of language spread invoke.3 Populations can switch language with little change in ancestry, and ancestry can spread without a language, as the Pacific case in the next lesson shows. They also cautioned that the Yamnaya individuals they sampled, from Samara, might not be directly ancestral to the German Corded Ware.4 What the genomes did was turn a large steppe migration from a hypothesis into an observation, which every theory of Indo-European origins now has to explain.

concepts.title: Proto-Indo-Anatolian and the Hybrid Hypothesis
concepts.contentHtml:
The two camps have begun to converge, though not on the same spot. In 2023 Heggarty's team, using their rebuilt database and sampled-ancestor trees, dated the family's root to about 8,120 years ago. That date is not consistent with the steppe hypothesis, but they argued it does not rule out a first homeland south of the Caucasus, with a later branch moving north onto the steppe and from there across Europe.1 They called this the hybrid hypothesis and presented it as a way to reconcile the language trees with ancient DNA from both the steppe and the northern Fertile Crescent.

In 2025 Lazaridis, Reich and colleagues replied with ancient DNA from 435 individuals. The Yamnaya culture appeared around 3300 BC on the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas and by 3000 BC stretched from Hungary to Kazakhstan.2 Its ancestors formed around 4000 BC among groups on the Dnipro and Don rivers, but about four-fifths of Yamnaya ancestry came from a Caucasus-lower Volga population. The same population contributed at least a tenth of the ancestry of Bronze Age central Anatolians, among whom Hittite was spoken.3 The authors therefore proposed that the final unity of the speakers of Proto-Indo-Anatolian, the ancestor of both Anatolian and Indo-European, lay among Caucasus-lower Volga people sometime between 4400 and 4000 BC.

Set side by side, the remaining disagreements are clear:

  • Where: both now look to the Caucasus region, but Heggarty's team allows a first homeland south of the mountains, while Lazaridis's team places it to the north, towards the lower Volga.
  • When: about 8,100 years ago from the vocabulary trees, against 4400–4000 BC, roughly 6,400–6,000 years ago, from the genetic model, with the Anatolian split itself dated linguistically to 4300–3500 BC.
  • Weak points: the genetic model has Anatolian speakers entering Anatolia probably from the east, yet there is no linguistic evidence of Anatolian speakers in eastern Anatolia along that path.4

Neither result is the last word, but every claim must now satisfy trees, words and genomes at once.

title: Austronesian and Bantu Expansions
description: Out of Taiwan by pulses and pauses, Bantu routes through the rainforest, and what genomes add

concepts.title: Out of Taiwan
concepts.contentHtml:
The Austronesian family, with around 1,000 to 1,200 languages, is one of the largest in the world. Its speakers spread from Taiwan into Island South-East Asia and across the Pacific, eventually reaching as far afield as Madagascar, Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand.1 Two scenarios competed to explain how. The pulse-pause scenario, sometimes called the express train, has Austronesian speakers originating in Taiwan around 5,500 years ago and spreading in rapid bursts. The slow-boat scenario argues for a much older origin in Island South-East Asia around 13,000–17,000 years ago, with one stream flowing north into Taiwan and another east into Oceania.

In 2009 Gray, Drummond and Greenhill used lexical data and Bayesian methods to build a tree of 400 Austronesian languages.2 Its four central findings each bear on the debate:

  • All the Formosan (aboriginal Taiwanese) languages sit at the base of the tree.
  • The tree is chained, stepping from Taiwan to the Philippines, Borneo and Sulawesi, Central Malayo-Polynesia, South Halmahera and West New Guinea, and finally Oceania.
  • The family's age is about 5,200 years, with a 95% interval of 4,750–5,800.
  • Branch lengths suggest a series of settlement pauses and expansion pulses.

The slow-boat scenario predicts both a different root and a far greater age, so the tree tells against it twice over. Critics replied by listing subgrouping errors, and the authors accepted that 25 of the 400 languages were not placed where linguistic evidence puts them.3 A few misplaced languages do not make a wrong tree, though. Measured over the whole posterior sample, the trees stayed close to the standard classification, and re-dating with only the most robust calibrations gave a mean age of 5,117 years. Y chromosome and whole-genome studies have also supported a Taiwanese origin, so here language trees and genes agree.4

concepts.title: Pauses, Social Life and the Lapita Genomes
concepts.contentHtml:
Why would an expansion pause? The 2009 study linked its pauses and pulses to technological and social innovations.1 Earlier work had already focused on three ancestral speech communities, each associated with an archaeological pause: Proto-Austronesian at the root in Taiwan; Proto-Malayo-Polynesian, before the move into the Philippines about 4,000–4,500 years ago; and Proto-Oceanic, about 3,500 years ago, associated with the Lapita culture and the spread into previously uninhabited Remote Oceania, including Polynesia.2 One reading is that migration paused while people acquired the sailing technology needed for further voyages.3

Once you have a dated tree, you can reconstruct more than words. Fiona Jordan and colleagues mapped where married couples lived in Austronesian societies onto the language trees and inferred the likely states of the ancestors. They found strong evidence that matrilocal residence, couples living with the wife's kin, was predominant in early Austronesian societies about 5,000–4,500 years ago, with posterior probabilities of 0.70 for Proto-Austronesian and 0.99 for Proto-Malayo-Polynesian.4 Patrilocality looks like a later development. This is the phylogenetic comparative method: the language tree serves as the family history against which cultural traits are tested.

Genomes then complicated the picture. In 2016 Pontus Skoglund and colleagues obtained genome-wide ancient DNA from three individuals from Vanuatu, dated to about 3,100–2,700 years ago, and one from Tonga, about 2,700–2,300 years ago. These early settlers had little to no Papuan ancestry.5 Yet indigenous people of the South Pacific today carry at least 25% Papuan ancestry. So later population movements spread Papuan ancestry through the region after the first settlement, while the islanders kept speaking Austronesian languages. Genes and languages can travel separately: a language tree is a history of languages, not automatically a history of populations.

concepts.title: Bantu: Through the Rainforest or Around It?
concepts.contentHtml:
More than 500 Bantu languages are spoken today by some 240 million people across 9 million square kilometres of sub-Saharan Africa.1 Their spread, which swept out of West Central Africa beginning around 5,000 years ago and carried a way of life in which farming played an increasingly important role, has been called the most dramatic demographic event in Late Holocene Africa.2 The homeland is generally placed near the border of Nigeria and Cameroon. The route is another matter. Did one early branch go east along the northern edge of the Congo rainforest while another went through it, or did the first migrants cross the forest before splitting?

Phylogeography gives different answers depending on the data and the model:

  • Thomas Currie and colleagues (2013) found that groups first moved south through the rainforest, and only after emerging on its south side split into western and eastern branches.3
  • Rebecca Grollemund and colleagues (2015), with a dated tree of about 400 languages, found that migrants did not spread in a random walk but followed emerging savannah corridors, and that moving from savannah into rainforest delayed settlement by about 300 years on average.4
  • Ezequiel Koile and colleagues (2022), using a break-away diffusion model designed for migrations, supported an expansion through the Central African forests about 4,420 years ago,5 well before the Sangha River Interval, a savannah corridor through the forest, was open.

Genetics offers an independent check. In 2024 Cesar Fortes-Lima, Carina Schlebusch and colleagues genotyped 1,763 people, including 1,526 Bantu speakers from 147 populations in 14 African countries, and sequenced 12 Late Iron Age genomes. Genetic diversity among Bantu-speaking populations declines with distance from western Africa,6 the signature of a serial-founder migration in which each new group carries a subset of the diversity of the one before. Bantu speakers also received significant gene flow from local groups in the regions they entered. The exact route through the forest is still debated, but the overall dispersal from the west now has support from linguistic, genetic and geographic data together.

title: Rates of Change and the Limits of Reconstruction
description: Why some words last for millennia, bursts at splits, fast-changing grammar, and how deep the signal goes

concepts.title: Fast Words, Slow Words
concepts.contentHtml:
Across more than 100 Indo-European languages and dialects, the meaning 'tail' is expressed by dozens of unrelated words, while every language uses a related form for 'two'. Glottochronology had treated such differences as noise. In 2007 Mark Pagel, Quentin Atkinson and Andrew Meade showed they are systematic. Using a database of 200 basic meanings in 87 Indo-European languages and word counts from large corpora of English, Spanish, Russian and Greek, they found that frequency of use predicts the rate of replacement: frequently used words evolve slowly and infrequently used words evolve rapidly.

The relationship held separately and identically across parts of speech in each of the four corpora, and it accounted for approximately 50% of the variation in historical rates of lexical replacement.1 Rates in this work are expressed as the expected number of replacements by a new, unrelated word per 1,000 years.2 The spread is huge. Most lexical items have short linguistic half-lives of just a few thousand years, but a smaller set evolves slowly enough to remain cognate across the time depths that separate whole language families.3 Low numbers such as 'two' belong to that slow set.

Why should frequency protect a word? The authors proposed that how often words are used in everyday language exerts a general and law-like influence on their rates of evolution, consistent with social models of word change that emphasise selection.4 One way to picture it: a word you say many times a day is reinforced constantly in every speaker, so a newcomer struggles to displace it, whereas a rarely used word is easily replaced. For phylogenetics the lesson is practical. Rate variation among meanings is real and partly predictable, so models must allow it, and the slow words are the ones that carry signal deepest into the past.

concepts.title: Bursts, Grammar and Lineages
concepts.contentHtml:
Change also depends on when in a lineage's life you look. Quentin Atkinson, Mark Pagel and colleagues asked whether languages change faster around the moments they split. Using vocabulary data from Bantu, Indo-European and Austronesian, they found that 10 to 33% of the overall vocabulary differences among these languages arose from rapid punctuational bursts of change associated with language-splitting events.1 They suggested a linguistic founder effect, or a desire to establish a distinct social identity. Either way, a lineage that has split many times will have accumulated extra change, which a simple clock would misread as extra time.

Many linguists hoped that grammar would change more slowly than words and so let them see further back. In 2017 Greenhill and colleagues tested this on 81 Austronesian languages, inferring rates of change in lexical and grammatical data with a Dirichlet process mixture model. On average, most grammatical features actually change faster than items of basic vocabulary.2 The grammatical data also showed less schismogenesis (change concentrated at splits), higher rates of homoplasy and more bursts of contact-induced change. There is a core of highly stable features in both grammar and vocabulary, but grammar as a whole is not a deeper clock. An earlier comparison found the same in tree shape: structural data were far less tree-like than basic vocabulary, with delta scores twice as large for Indo-European.3

Even word-order universals look less universal on a tree. Generative linguists following Chomsky argued that innate parameters constrain diversity, while linguists following Greenberg pointed to statistical tendencies for traits to occur together. In 2011 Michael Dunn and colleagues tested both with phylogenetic methods. Only a few word-order features evolved in strongly correlated ways, against the parameter view, and most dependencies between traits were lineage-specific rather than universal, against the Greenbergian one.4 At least for word order, each family seems to follow its own path, with the current state of a language shaping where it can go next.

concepts.title: How Deep Can We See?
concepts.contentHtml:
Most words evolve too rapidly to preserve evidence of their ancestry beyond about 5,000 to 9,000 years,1 and the comparative method is commonly thought to reach its limit somewhere between 6,000 and 10,000 years.2 Can statistics see past that barrier? In 2013 Pagel, Atkinson, Andreea Calude and Meade argued that it can, for a small set of ultraconserved words. They took proposed proto-words for the 200 Swadesh meanings from the Languages of the World Etymological Database for seven Eurasian language families, postulated to form a superfamily, often called Eurasiatic, that evolved from a common ancestor around 15,000 years ago.

Their model, which takes into account how often words are used in everyday speech, predicted which meanings should show deep cognates, and the data fitted: words used more than once per 1,000 in everyday speech were 7 to 10 times more likely to show deep ancestry.3 Their dated tree gave the superfamily a time depth of about 14,450 years, implying that some frequently used words have been retained in related forms since the end of the last ice age.4

Paul Heggarty's response was blunt. The "data", he argued, were subjective interpretations by the Moscow school behind the database, widely rejected by specialists in language reconstruction. Proto-lexicons are already biased towards stable meanings, because those are easiest to reconstruct, so finding a stability signal is "correlation in, correlation out". Above all, stability in meaning is powerless against instability in sound:5 Latin [akwam], 'water', became French [o] in just two millennia. Whether enough phonetic signal survives to judge cognacy back to 14,450 years is exactly what needs testing, he wrote, and pushing it back 70 millennia would be like trying to radiocarbon date something about 300,000 years old.6 Pagel's team replied that no evidence had been provided for these problems. The debate marks the frontier: the depth limit is set by how fast sounds erode, and whether any method can reliably detect cognates beyond it remains an open question.
